title: Standard Operating Procedure: Incoming Goods Inspection

content.text: Standard Operating Procedure: Incoming Goods Inspection

This standard operating procedure describes how deliveries of purchased materials and components are accepted, checked and released at the goods receipt of [ORG_1]. Its aim is to ensure that only materials that meet the agreed specifications are used in the production of electric drive components, such as motors, gearboxes and frequency inverters. Nonconforming materials must be detected as early as possible, before they cause scrap, rework or customer complaints.

The procedure also ensures that every delivery is traceable from the supplier to the finished product, as required by our quality management system and by the contracts with our automotive and mechanical engineering customers.

This procedure applies to all deliveries of production materials received at the central goods receipt of the plant in [LOCATION_1]. This includes raw materials such as copper wire and electrical steel, purchased parts such as bearings, shafts and housings, electronic components and packaging materials that come into direct contact with the product.

It does not apply to deliveries of office supplies, tools, spare parts for maintenance or capital goods. These are accepted by the requesting department in accordance with the procurement guideline. Deliveries to the external warehouse in [LOCATION_2] are covered by a separate procedure, SOP-LOG-007.
The following roles are involved in the incoming goods inspection:
accept deliveries, check delivery documents and packaging, post the goods receipt in the ERP system and move the goods to the inspection area or to stock.
carry out the sampling inspection according to the inspection plan, document the results and decide on the release or blocking of a batch.
ensures that sufficient staff and space are available at the goods receipt and that blocked goods are stored separately.
maintains the inspection plans, evaluates inspection results and handles complaints with suppliers.
owns this procedure, decides on special releases and approves changes to inspection plans.

All employees who carry out inspections must have completed the training on this procedure and the instruction on the measuring equipment they use. Training records are kept by the quality department.
a quantity of material of the same type, produced by the supplier under uniform conditions and delivered with a single batch number.
the quantity of material from one delivery that is subject to a joint inspection decision; normally identical to one batch.
an inspection of a defined number of parts taken at random from the inspection lot, in accordance with the sampling plan.
a reduced inspection frequency for suppliers and materials with a proven record of good quality; only every fifth lot is inspected.
a complete inspection of all characteristics on the first delivery of a new or changed part.
a documented decision to use material that does not fully meet the specification, approved by the Head of Quality Assurance.
stock that is physically separated and blocked in the ERP system and must not be used in production.

The incoming goods inspection is carried out in four steps: delivery acceptance, visual and document check, sampling inspection and release or blocking. The individual steps are described below. Deliveries must be processed within one working day of arrival, and deliveries of materials marked as urgent in the ERP system within four hours.
Check the delivery note against the open purchase order in the ERP system.
Compare the supplier, material number, quantity and order number.
If there is no matching purchase order, contact the responsible buyer before unloading.
Check the number of packages against the delivery note and the carrier's consignment note.
Inspect the outer packaging for damage, moisture or signs of tampering.
Photograph any damage and note it on the consignment note before the driver leaves.
Have the driver countersign the note.
Unload the goods and place them in the marked goods receipt area.
Post the goods receipt in the ERP system with reference to the purchase order.

If the delivery is incomplete or damaged, the goods receipt staff inform the responsible buyer by email on the same day. Deliveries that are clearly unusable may be refused in agreement with the buyer.
Check that each package is labelled with the material number, batch number, quantity and date of manufacture.
Check that the required certificates are enclosed.
Inspection certificate 3.1 for copper wire, electrical steel and shafts.
Certificate of conformity for electronic components.
Material safety data sheet for chemicals and adhesives on first delivery.
Compare the certificate values with the specification limits in the inspection plan.
Check the inner packaging and a sample of the parts for visible damage, corrosion and contamination.
Scan the certificates and attach them to the goods receipt in the document management system.
Missing or incorrect certificates are a reason for blocking the batch, even if the parts themselves are in order. The supplier quality engineer requests the missing documents from the supplier.

The ERP system automatically creates an inspection lot for each goods receipt of an inspection-relevant material. The quality inspector takes the samples, carries out the inspections defined in the inspection plan and records the results directly in the inspection lot. The sample size depends on the lot size and the inspection level and is calculated by the system based on the sampling plan.
The most important inspection characteristics for typical materials are listed in the following table. The complete inspection plans are stored in the ERP system.
No solder defects, correct component placement

All measuring equipment used for incoming inspection must be included in the calibration management system and bear a valid calibration label. Before each measurement, the quality inspector checks the calibration status. If a measuring instrument is found to be out of calibration, all measurements taken with it since the last valid calibration must be assessed by the supplier quality engineer, and the affected lots may have to be re-inspected.
If a single nonconforming part is found in the sample, the sample size is doubled. If a nonconforming part is found in the extended sample, the entire lot is blocked.
If all inspection results meet the acceptance criteria, the quality inspector makes the usage decision "accepted" in the ERP system.
The stock is automatically transferred from inspection stock to unrestricted stock.
The goods receipt staff move the material to its storage location.
If an inspection result does not meet the acceptance criteria, the quality inspector makes the usage decision "rejected".
The stock is transferred to blocked stock.
The material is labelled with a red blocking label and moved to the locked blocking area.
The supplier quality engineer is informed automatically.
If production urgently needs the material, a special release can be requested in accordance with section 6.
The goods receipt is only complete when a usage decision has been made. Inspection lots without a usage decision for more than three working days are reported in the daily quality meeting.
Some deliveries require a different handling than the standard procedure described above:
First deliveries of new or changed parts:
a first article inspection of all drawing characteristics is carried out. The goods remain blocked until the supplier quality engineer has approved the initial sample inspection report.
the goods receipt is posted as usual, but the ERP system only creates an inspection lot for every fifth delivery. All other deliveries are released after the visual and document check.
the goods receipt staff inform the quality inspector by phone so that the inspection can be carried out with priority. Urgency does not justify skipping any inspection step.
these are not handled at the goods receipt for purchased materials but are forwarded to the complaints area of the quality department.
the night shift supervisor accepts the delivery, checks the delivery note and packaging and leaves the goods in the goods receipt area for inspection on the next working day.

Nonconforming goods are handled in accordance with the procedure for nonconforming products, SOP-QM-009. The supplier quality engineer creates a supplier complaint in the ERP system within two working days and informs the supplier. The complaint contains a description of the defect, photos, measurement results and the affected quantity. The supplier must submit an initial response with containment measures within 48 hours and a complete 8D report within 15 working days.
Depending on the type of defect and the urgency, the following options are available:
Return of the complete batch to the supplier at the supplier's expense
Sorting or rework by the supplier at our premises, under the supervision of a quality inspector
Sorting by our own staff, with the costs charged to the supplier
Special release for use, if the deviation does not affect form, fit or function, approved by the Head of Quality Assurance and, where required by contract, by the customer
Scrapping, documented with a scrap report

All costs caused by nonconforming deliveries, such as sorting, additional transport and production downtime, are charged to the supplier in accordance with the quality assurance agreement. Repeated defects are taken into account in the quarterly supplier evaluation and may lead to an escalation to a supplier development programme.

The results of all incoming inspections are recorded in the ERP system and linked to the inspection lot, the goods receipt and the batch. The following records must be kept for at least 15 years, in accordance with the requirements of our customers in the automotive industry:
Delivery notes and goods receipt postings
Certificates and test reports of the supplier
Special releases with the corresponding approvals

The quality department evaluates the incoming inspection results monthly. The evaluation includes the rejection rate per supplier and material group, the average processing time at the goods receipt and the number of open inspection lots. The results are presented in the monthly quality report and used to adjust inspection levels. A supplier that has had no rejection for twelve consecutive lots can be switched to skip-lot inspection. After a rejection, the supplier automatically returns to normal inspection.
